specStatements.text: Students should be able to:
• give examples of the forces involved in stretching, bending or compressing an object
• explain why, to change the shape of an object (by stretching, bending or compressing), more than one force has to be applied – this is limited to stationary objects only
• describe the difference between elastic deformation and inelastic deformation caused by stretching forces.
The extension of an elastic object, such as a spring, is directly proportional to the force applied, provided that the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
force = spring constant × extension
[F = k e]
force, F, in newtons, N
spring constant, k, in newtons per metre, N/m
extension, e, in metres, m
This relationship also applies to the compression of an elastic object, where ‘ e ’ would be the compression of the object.

A force that stretches (or compresses) a spring does work and elastic potential energy is stored in the spring. Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done on the spring and the elastic potential energy stored are equal.
Students should be able to:
• describe the difference between a linear and non-linear relationship between force and extension
• calculate a spring constant in linear cases
• interpret data from an investigation of the relationship between force and extension
• calculate work done in stretching (or compressing) a spring (up to the limit of proportionality) using the equation:elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2[E_e = 1/2 k e^2]
Students should be able to calculate relevant values of stored energy and energy transfers.
Required practical activity 6: investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 2.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

scopeNotes.statement: this is limited to stationary objects only
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every situation used to explain why more than one force is needed involves an object that stays stationary while its shape changes: a rubber band held between a clamp and a hand, a suspension spring under a parked car, a spring hanging at rest from a stand. No item asks what happens when a single force acts on a free object that is allowed to accelerate, and no item asks about the deformation of a moving object. The reasoning offered is the specification's own: a single force would leave a resultant force, so a stationary object could not stay stationary.

Every calculation using E_e = 1/2 k e^2, and every calculation using F = k e, is set below the limit of proportionality, and each stem says so or supplies data that lies on the straight part of the graph. Beyond the limit of proportionality the treatment is qualitative only: students are asked what the curved region of a graph shows and how work done then compares with the energy stored, never to compute a value of stored energy there.

concepts.definition: A change in the shape of an object caused by forces acting on it. An object may be deformed by stretching it, by bending it or by compressing (squashing) it.
Making an object longer by pulling its ends apart. Examples include a rubber band pulled between two hands and a spring hanging from a stand with a weight on the end.
Making an object shorter by pushing its ends towards each other. Examples include the suspension spring of a parked car and a spring squashed between a hand and the bench.
Changing the shape of an object so that one side is stretched while the other side is compressed, for example a diving board pushed down at the free end while the fixed end is held.

concepts.term: Why more than one force is needed
concepts.definition: To change the shape of a stationary object, more than one force must be applied. A single force would produce a resultant force, and the object would accelerate away instead of changing shape.
Deformation from which an object returns to its original shape and length once the deforming forces are removed.
Deformation after which an object does not return to its original shape and length when the deforming forces are removed; it stays permanently changed.
The increase in length of an object compared with its original, unloaded length. Extension = stretched length - original length.
Two quantities are directly proportional when a graph of one against the other is a straight line through the origin, so doubling one doubles the other.
The point beyond which the extension of an object is no longer directly proportional to the force applied. Up to this point the force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin.
The relationship between the force applied to an elastic object and its extension, written as F = k e. It holds up to the limit of proportionality.
The force applied to the spring, measured in newtons, N. For a spring hanging from a stand with masses on it, this force is the weight of the masses.
A measure of the stiffness of a spring: the force needed per metre of extension, measured in newtons per metre, N/m. A stiffer spring has a larger spring constant.
The extension used in F = k e, measured in metres, m. Lengths measured in centimetres or millimetres must be converted to metres before the equation is used.
The same relationship applies when an elastic object is compressed. In that case e stands for the compression of the object rather than its extension.

concepts.term: Work done and elastic potential energy
concepts.definition: A force that stretches or compresses a spring does work, and elastic potential energy is stored in the spring. Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done and the energy stored are equal.
A linear force-extension relationship gives a straight-line graph, so equal increases in force give equal increases in extension. A non-linear relationship gives a curve.
For a linear region, plotting force on the vertical axis against extension on the horizontal axis gives a straight line whose gradient is the spring constant, k.
The energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring, E_e = 1/2 k e^2, valid up to the limit of proportionality. Energy is in joules, J.
When a stretched or compressed spring is released, the elastic potential energy stored in it is transferred to other stores, for example to the kinetic energy store of an object it pushes.

An investigation of the relationship between force and extension for a spring: hang the spring from a stand, add known weights one at a time, and measure the length after each weight so that the extension can be found.

concepts.term: AT 1 and AT 2 in this practical
concepts.definition: AT 1 is the use of apparatus to make length measurements; AT 2 is the safe use of apparatus to measure force. Both are used when a ruler and known weights are used on a loaded spring.

concepts.term: Working scientifically and maths skills here
concepts.definition: The practical develops skills such as tabulating results, plotting force against extension, drawing a line of best fit, finding a gradient and identifying anomalous results.

misconceptions.question: How many forces must act on a stationary object to change its shape?
misconceptions.correct: More than one force must act on it.
misconceptions.misconception: Only one force is needed – you just pull the spring and it stretches.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language you pull a spring with one hand and it stretches, so the second force, supplied by whatever holds the other end, is never noticed.
misconceptions.correction: If a single force acted there would be a resultant force and the stationary object would accelerate away instead of changing shape. The clamp, hand or bench at the other end always supplies a second force.

misconceptions.question: Two forces act on a rubber band. Will they always stretch it?
misconceptions.correct: Only if they act in opposite directions, pulling the two ends apart.
misconceptions.misconception: Any two forces will stretch it, because more than one force is acting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is memorised as a count of forces, so the direction of each force is never checked.
misconceptions.correction: Two forces acting the same way would give a resultant force and move the band. To stretch it the forces must pull the ends in opposite directions; to compress it they must push the ends together.

misconceptions.question: Can a steel spring be deformed elastically?
misconceptions.correct: Yes – elastic deformation is about behaviour, not about the material.
misconceptions.misconception: No – elastic means rubbery, so only rubber-like materials are elastic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday word 'elastic' names a material (an elastic band), so the physics meaning gets attached to soft, stretchy substances.
misconceptions.correction: In physics, elastic deformation means the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed. A steel spring does exactly that, so it is behaving elastically.

misconceptions.question: What does inelastic deformation mean?
misconceptions.correct: The object does not return to its original shape when the force is removed.
misconceptions.misconception: The object snaps or breaks into pieces.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Inelastic' sounds like failure, and the most memorable way a stretched object can fail is by breaking.
misconceptions.correction: Inelastic deformation means a permanent change of shape: the object stays longer or bent after the force is removed. It is still in one piece.

misconceptions.question: A spring 5.0 cm long stretches to 8.5 cm. What is the extension?
misconceptions.correct: The extension is 3.5 cm, the increase in length.
misconceptions.misconception: The extension is 8.5 cm, because that is how long the stretched spring is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'extension' is heard as 'the extended length', and the stretched length is the number the ruler shows.
misconceptions.correction: Extension is the increase in length: stretched length - original length. Here that is 8.5 - 5.0 = 3.5 cm, which is 0.035 m.

misconceptions.question: Does F = k e work for any force applied to a spring?
misconceptions.correct: Only up to the limit of proportionality.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes – it is the spring equation, so it works for every load.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Equations are learnt as unconditional rules, and the proviso in the specification is easy to drop when recalling the formula.
misconceptions.correction: Beyond the limit of proportionality extension is no longer directly proportional to force, the graph curves, and F = k e no longer gives the right answer.

misconceptions.question: What happens at the limit of proportionality?
misconceptions.correct: Extension stops being directly proportional to the force.
misconceptions.misconception: The spring snaps and can no longer carry a load.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Limit' is read as the end of the spring's useful life, so it is confused with the breaking point.
misconceptions.correction: At the limit of proportionality the graph stops being a straight line. The spring can still be stretched further; it just extends by more per newton, and it may become inelastically deformed.

misconceptions.question: In what unit is the spring constant measured?
misconceptions.correct: Newtons per metre, N/m.
misconceptions.misconception: Newtons, N, because it appears in a force equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every symbol in F = k e is associated with the force being calculated, and N is the unit that comes to mind for anything to do with springs.
misconceptions.correction: The spring constant is a force per unit extension, so its unit is newtons per metre, N/m. Only F is in newtons.

misconceptions.question: Spring A has k = 30 N/m and spring B has k = 90 N/m. Under the same force, which extends more?
misconceptions.correct: Spring A, because it has the smaller spring constant.
misconceptions.misconception: Spring B, because a bigger spring constant means a bigger extension.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A large number is read as 'more of everything', so a large k is assumed to mean a large stretch.
misconceptions.correction: Rearranging F = k e gives e = F / k, so for the same force a larger spring constant gives a smaller extension. A large k means a stiff spring that is hard to stretch.

misconceptions.question: The extension of a spring is doubled below the limit of proportionality. What happens to the energy stored?
misconceptions.correct: It becomes four times as large.
misconceptions.misconception: It doubles, because the extension has doubled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Proportional reasoning learnt from F = k e is carried over to the energy equation without noticing the extension is squared.
misconceptions.correction: E_e = 1/2 k e^2, so the energy depends on the square of the extension. Doubling e multiplies the stored energy by 2^2 = 4.

misconceptions.question: A force of 6.0 N stretches a spring by 12 cm. What is k?
misconceptions.correct: 50 N/m, using an extension of 0.12 m.
misconceptions.misconception: 0.50 N/m, from 6.0 divided by 12.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The centimetre figure is used straight from the table, because the equation does not look as though it cares about units.
misconceptions.correction: The extension must be in metres: 12 cm = 0.12 m, so k = 6.0 / 0.12 = 50 N/m.

misconceptions.question: Does F = k e apply to a compressed spring?
misconceptions.correct: Yes – e is then the compression of the spring.
misconceptions.misconception: No – a different equation is needed for squashing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is always met in the context of stretching, so compression is assumed to be a separate case with its own rule.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the relationship also applies to compression, with e standing for the compression of the object.

misconceptions.question: A spring is stretched elastically. How does the energy stored compare with the work done?
misconceptions.correct: They are equal.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy stored is a little less, because some energy is always wasted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule that energy transfers are never fully useful is applied here, even though the specification states the two are equal for a spring that is not inelastically deformed.
misconceptions.correction: Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done on the spring and the elastic potential energy stored in it are equal.

misconceptions.question: A force-extension graph curves at high loads. What does the curve show?
misconceptions.correct: The limit of proportionality has been passed.
misconceptions.misconception: The readings there are wrong and should be discarded as anomalies.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are told to look for anomalies and to expect a straight line, so any departure from a straight line is read as experimental error.
misconceptions.correction: A smooth, repeatable curve at the top of the graph is real physics: beyond the limit of proportionality the extension is no longer proportional to the force. An anomaly is a single point off an otherwise smooth trend.

misconceptions.question: Beyond the limit of proportionality the graph bends towards the extension axis. What does this mean?
misconceptions.correct: The spring extends more for each extra newton than it did before.
misconceptions.misconception: The spring is getting stiffer as the load grows.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any bend in a graph is read as 'harder', and a stretched spring feels tighter, so 'stiffer' seems the natural description.
misconceptions.correction: The graph bending away from the straight line means each extra newton now produces a larger extension than before, so the spring is easier, not harder, to stretch further.

misconceptions.question: What does the area under a linear force-extension graph give?
misconceptions.correct: The work done, which equals the elastic potential energy stored.
misconceptions.misconception: The spring constant of the spring.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gradient and area are both 'things you get off a graph', and the spring constant is the quantity most associated with this graph.
misconceptions.correction: The gradient gives the spring constant; the area under the line gives the work done on the spring, which equals the energy stored.

misconceptions.question: A spring hangs from a stand with a weight on the end. Which forces stretch it?
misconceptions.correct: The weight pulls down and the stand pulls up.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the weight acts, and that alone stretches the spring.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The weight is the force the student adds and can see, while the upward pull of the stand on the top of the spring is invisible and easy to ignore.
misconceptions.correction: The stand supplies an equal upward force on the top of the spring. Two forces act in opposite directions, which is why the spring stretches instead of accelerating downwards.

misconceptions.question: How is the energy stored in a stretched spring calculated?
misconceptions.correct: Using E_e = 1/2 k e^2.
misconceptions.misconception: By multiplying the force by the extension.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Work done = force × distance is applied directly, ignoring that the force grows from zero as the spring stretches.
misconceptions.correction: The force increases from zero as the spring stretches, so the energy stored is 1/2 k e^2, which is half of F e for a linear spring.

misconceptions.question: A spring is stretched until it is inelastically deformed. Is the work done still equal to the energy stored?
misconceptions.correct: No – the work done is greater than the elastic potential energy stored.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes – work done always equals the elastic potential energy stored.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The statement 'work done = energy stored' is remembered without the condition attached to it in the specification.
misconceptions.correction: The equality holds only if the spring is not inelastically deformed. When it is permanently deformed, some of the work done is transferred to the thermal energy store instead of being stored elastically.

misconceptions.question: Is energy stored in a spring that is compressed?
misconceptions.correct: Yes – elastic potential energy is stored when it is compressed as well.
misconceptions.misconception: No – energy is only stored when a spring is stretched.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Storing energy is pictured as 'pulling something back', so squashing does not look like a way of storing energy.
misconceptions.correction: A force that compresses a spring does work on it, so elastic potential energy is stored, and it is released when the spring pushes back.

misconceptions.question: A spring is held stretched by a steady force. Has work been done on it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes – work was done while it was being stretched.
misconceptions.misconception: No – the spring is not moving, so no work has been done.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Work is linked to visible motion, and a stretched spring held still looks like a situation with no movement at all.
misconceptions.correction: Work is done while the spring is being extended, because the applied force moves through a distance. That work is stored as elastic potential energy.

misconceptions.question: How should the ruler be read when measuring the length of a loaded spring?
misconceptions.correct: At eye level, with the ruler vertical next to the spring.
misconceptions.misconception: From wherever you happen to be sitting; eye position cannot change a ruler reading.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The scale looks like a fixed, objective thing, so the idea that the reading depends on the line of sight is not obvious.
misconceptions.correction: Reading from above or below causes a parallax error. The ruler should be vertical, clamped next to the spring, and read at eye level.

misconceptions.question: How is the length of the loaded spring measured in the practical?
misconceptions.correct: With the spring still hanging, using a ruler clamped beside it.
misconceptions.misconception: By taking the spring off the stand and laying it flat on the bench.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Measuring something lying on the bench feels easier and more accurate than measuring something hanging in mid-air.
misconceptions.correction: The spring must be measured while the load is still on it, because removing the load lets the spring return to its original length and the extension is lost.

misconceptions.question: Why must a second force be applied to deform a stationary object?
misconceptions.correct: Because a single force would leave a resultant force and the object would accelerate.
misconceptions.misconception: Because forces come in pairs anyway, so a second force appears by itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Newton's third law is remembered as 'forces come in pairs', which is then used to explain away the need to apply a second force.
misconceptions.correction: The two forces that deform an object act on the same object and must both be applied to it. A third-law pair acts on two different objects and could not squash or stretch anything on its own.

misconceptions.question: Two springs are given the same force. Do they extend by the same amount?
misconceptions.correct: No – the extension also depends on the spring constant.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes – the same force always produces the same extension.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Force is treated as the only thing that matters, so the stiffness of the spring drops out of the reasoning.
misconceptions.correction: From e = F / k, the same force gives a smaller extension in a spring with a larger spring constant.

misconceptions.question: A spring returns to its original length after the force is removed. What was this?
misconceptions.correct: Elastic deformation.
misconceptions.misconception: Inelastic deformation, because the spring did change shape while the force acted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two terms are learnt as a pair and the labels are attached to the wrong behaviour, especially as every deformation involves a change of shape.
misconceptions.correction: The test is what happens after the force is removed: returning to the original shape is elastic deformation; staying deformed is inelastic deformation.

misconceptions.question: A spring has k = 120 N/m and an extension of 0.25 m. How is the force found?
misconceptions.correct: By multiplying: F = k e = 120 × 0.25.
misconceptions.misconception: By dividing the two numbers, because that is what you do with an equation like this.
misconceptions.whyItArises: F = k e is remembered as a formula triangle and the division is carried out the wrong way round, especially when one number is smaller than one.
misconceptions.correction: F is already the subject of the equation, so k and e are multiplied. Division is used only when F is known and k or e is being found.

mcqs.stem: A rubber band is held by a clamp at one end while a student pulls the other end, and the band stretches. Which statement describes the forces that stretch the band?

options.text: Two forces act on the band, pulling its two ends in opposite directions.
options.rationale: Deforming a stationary object needs more than one force, and to stretch it the forces must pull the ends apart.

options.text: One pulling force acts on the band, along the line of the band.
options.rationale: Students count only the pull they are consciously applying and forget the clamp.

options.text: Two forces act on the band, both pulling it towards the clamp.
options.rationale: The 'more than one force' rule is recalled as a count, without checking directions.

options.text: The weight of the band is the only force acting, and it stretches it.
options.rationale: Weight is the force named first for anything held or hanging.

mcqs.stem: A car is parked on level ground and the springs in its suspension are squashed. Which pair of forces compresses one of these springs?

options.text: The weight of the car is the only force acting on the spring.
options.rationale: Weight is offered as a complete explanation for anything a heavy object does.

options.text: The car body pushes down on the spring and the axle pushes up on it.
options.rationale: Compression needs two forces pushing the ends of the spring towards each other.

options.text: The car body and the axle both push down on the spring from above it.
options.rationale: Two forces are named, but both in the same direction, which would move the spring.

options.text: The spring squashes under its own weight as it hangs there.
options.rationale: A single force is treated as enough to change the shape of the spring.

mcqs.stem: Why must more than one force be applied to a stationary object in order to change its shape?

options.text: A single force on its own is enough to stretch the object into a new shape.
options.rationale: Reflects the belief that one force alone suffices to change an object's shape.

options.text: Forces always occur in pairs, so a second force appears without being applied.
options.rationale: Newton's third law is used to supply the second force automatically.

options.text: A single force would leave a resultant force, so the object would accelerate.
options.rationale: With one force there is a resultant force; the object would move off rather than deform, so a second force is needed.

options.text: One force by itself will stretch the object, so no second force is needed.
options.rationale: Holds that a single applied force stretches the object, needing no second force.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes elastic deformation?

options.text: The object keeps part of its extra length after the forces are removed.
options.rationale: This describes inelastic deformation; the two labels are swapped.

options.text: The object is made of rubber, so it stretches much further than metal does.
options.rationale: 'Elastic' is treated as the name of a material rather than a behaviour.

options.text: The object breaks into pieces as soon as the stretching force is removed.
options.rationale: Deformation is confused with failure of the material.

options.text: The object returns to its original shape once the forces are removed.
options.rationale: Elastic deformation is defined by full recovery of the original shape when the forces are removed.

mcqs.stem: A steel spring is stretched by a very large force. When the force is removed the spring is longer than it was at the start. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It has been elastically deformed, because its shape changed while pulled.
options.rationale: Elastic is defined by 'it changed shape', not by what happens afterwards.

options.text: It has been inelastically deformed, so it has not returned to its original shape.
options.rationale: Not returning to the original length after the force is removed is exactly inelastic deformation.

options.text: It cannot have deformed elastically, since steel is not a stretchy material.
options.rationale: The behaviour is judged from the material rather than from the recovery.

options.text: It has been inelastically deformed, so the metal has begun to break apart.
options.rationale: The right term is chosen but explained as the spring starting to snap.

mcqs.stem: A spring is loaded with weights, staying below its limit of proportionality. Which statement about the force and the extension is correct?

options.text: The extension is directly proportional to the total length of the spring used.
options.rationale: Extension is confused with the length of the stretched spring.

options.text: The force is proportional to the extension whatever the load size.
options.rationale: The proviso about the limit of proportionality is dropped.

options.text: The extension is directly proportional to the force applied to the spring.
options.rationale: This is the specification statement: extension is directly proportional to force below the limit of proportionality.

options.text: The extension is proportional to the spring constant of that spring.
options.rationale: A larger spring constant is assumed to mean a larger extension.

mcqs.stem: What does the limit of proportionality of a spring tell you?

options.text: The force at which the spring finally snaps and can carry no more load.
options.rationale: 'Limit' is read as the breaking point of the spring.

options.text: The force beyond which the spring will not return to its original length.
options.rationale: This describes the elastic limit, not the limit of proportionality.

options.text: The largest length the spring reaches before it stops stretching.
options.rationale: The limit is treated as a length rather than as a force.

options.text: The largest force for which extension stays proportional to force.
options.rationale: Up to this force the graph is a straight line through the origin; beyond it, proportionality is lost.

mcqs.stem: A spring has a spring constant of 120 N/m and is stretched by 25 cm, which is below its limit of proportionality. Using force = spring constant × extension, what is the force applied to the spring?

options.rationale: The extension is used in centimetres: 120 × 25.
The equation is rearranged the wrong way: 120 / 0.25.
The reciprocal is taken: 0.25 / 120.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the quantities in the equation F = k e is correct?

options.text: The spring constant, k, is measured in newtons, N, as a force is.
options.rationale: Everything in the equation is assumed to be measured in newtons.

options.text: The extension, e, is measured in centimetres, cm, in this equation.
options.rationale: Extensions are usually recorded in centimetres, so cm is assumed to be fine.

options.text: The spring constant, k, is measured in newtons per metre, written N/m.
options.rationale: F is in newtons, k is in newtons per metre and e is in metres.

options.text: The extension, e, is the whole length of the stretched spring.
options.rationale: Extension is confused with the stretched length.

mcqs.stem: A force of 6.0 N stretches a spring by 12 cm. The limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. What is the spring constant of this spring?

options.rationale: The extension is left in centimetres: 6.0 / 12.
The equation is inverted and the centimetre value used: 12 / 6.0.
The value is right but the spring constant is given the unit of force.

options.text: 50 N/m

mcqs.stem: Spring A has a spring constant of 30 N/m and spring B has a spring constant of 90 N/m. The same force is applied to each spring. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Spring B extends less, because a larger spring constant means a stiffer spring.
options.rationale: Since e = F / k, a larger spring constant gives a smaller extension for the same force.

options.text: Spring B extends more, because a larger spring constant means more stretch.
options.rationale: A larger value of k is read as 'stretches more'.

options.text: Both springs extend by exactly the same amount, because the same force is applied.
options.rationale: The stiffness of the spring is left out of the reasoning.

options.text: Spring B extends three times as far as spring A does under this force.
options.rationale: The ratio of spring constants is applied the wrong way round.

mcqs.stem: A spring is squashed rather than stretched. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A different equation is needed, because F = k e only covers stretching.
options.rationale: The equation is tied to the stretching situations in which it is met.

options.text: F = k e still applies, with e as the compression of the spring.
options.rationale: The specification states that the relationship also applies to compression, with e as the compression.

options.text: No energy is stored, because energy is only stored by stretching a spring.
options.rationale: Storing energy is pictured as pulling something back.

options.text: The spring constant becomes negative when the spring is compressed.
options.rationale: The change of direction is transferred to the spring constant.

mcqs.stem: A spring is stretched by a force and is not inelastically deformed. How does the elastic potential energy stored compare with the work done on the spring?

options.text: The energy stored is slightly less, because some energy is wasted.
options.rationale: The rule that transfers are never fully useful is applied here.

options.text: The energy stored is much smaller, because a lot of energy is wasted.
options.rationale: Assumes wasted energy makes the stored energy much smaller than the work done.

options.text: No work is done at all, because the spring stays in one place.
options.rationale: Work is linked to visible movement of the whole object.

options.text: The energy stored is equal to the work done on the spring by the force.
options.rationale: The specification states that the work done and the elastic potential energy stored are equal in this case.

mcqs.stem: A spring is stretched so far that it is inelastically deformed. Which statement about the work done on the spring is correct?

options.text: The work done is greater than the elastic potential energy stored in it.
options.rationale: The equality holds only when the spring is not inelastically deformed; here some work is transferred elsewhere.

options.text: The work done is still exactly equal to the elastic potential energy stored.
options.rationale: The equality is remembered without the condition attached to it.

options.text: The work done equals the energy stored, because they are always the same.
options.rationale: Assumes work always equals elastic potential energy, even after inelastic deformation.

options.text: No work is done, because the spring does not spring back again.
options.rationale: Work done is judged from whether the spring recovers.

mcqs.stem: A force-extension graph for a spring is a straight line through the origin up to 8 N, and curves above 8 N. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The curved readings are anomalies and should be left out of the graph.
options.rationale: Treats the curved readings as anomalies to be discarded from the graph.

options.text: The relationship is linear up to 8 N and non-linear above 8 N.
options.rationale: A straight line through the origin is a linear relationship; the curved region above 8 N is non-linear.

options.text: The curved part shows the spring becoming stiffer as the load increases.
options.rationale: A bend in the graph is read as the spring getting harder to stretch.

options.text: The curved part is caused by measurement errors in the larger readings.
options.rationale: A departure from a straight line is read as experimental error.

mcqs.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 2000 N/m is stretched by 8.0 cm, below its limit of proportionality. Using elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2, how much energy is stored?

options.rationale: The extension is used in centimetres: 0.5 × 2000 × 8.0^2.
The factor of 0.5 is left out: 2000 × 0.080^2.
The extension is not squared: 0.5 × 2000 × 0.080.

mcqs.stem: The extension of a spring is doubled, and the spring stays below its limit of proportionality. What happens to the elastic potential energy stored in it?

options.text: It becomes four times as large, because the extension is squared.
options.rationale: E_e = 1/2 k e^2, so multiplying e by 2 multiplies the stored energy by 4.

options.text: It doubles, because the energy is proportional to the extension.
options.rationale: The proportionality in F = k e is carried over to the energy equation.

options.text: It stays the same, because the spring constant has not changed.
options.rationale: The spring constant is treated as the only thing that sets the energy.

options.text: It doubles too, because the energy just follows the extension.
options.rationale: Takes energy as proportional to extension, so doubling extension doubles the energy.

mcqs.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 800 N/m is compressed by 3.0 cm and then released, pushing a trolley along a smooth bench. Which statement describes the main energy transfer?

options.text: The compressed spring holds no energy, so nothing moves the trolley.
options.rationale: Assumes a compressed spring stores no energy, so nothing is transferred to the trolley.

options.text: No energy is transferred, because a compressed spring stores no energy.
options.rationale: Energy storage is associated only with stretching.

options.text: The elastic potential energy store of the spring empties to the kinetic store.
options.rationale: Releasing the spring transfers the stored elastic potential energy to the kinetic energy store of the trolley.

options.text: The energy stored is transferred to the thermal store of the bench.
options.rationale: Every transfer is assumed to end up as wasted thermal energy.

mcqs.stem: In an investigation of force and extension, a student records: 1.0 N, 2.0 cm; 2.0 N, 4.0 cm; 3.0 N, 6.0 cm; 4.0 N, 8.0 cm; 5.0 N, 12.0 cm. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: All five points fit a straight line, so k is 50 N/m for the spring.
options.rationale: The final point is assumed to fit because the graph is expected to be straight.

options.text: The first four points give k = 50 N/m, and the last point is off the line.
options.rationale: The first four points give a constant 2.0 cm per newton, so k = 1.0 / 0.020 = 50 N/m, and the 5.0 N point does not fit.

options.text: The spring constant is 0.42 N/m, taken from the last pair of readings.
options.rationale: One reading is used and the extension is left in centimetres: 5.0 / 12.0.

options.text: The spring became stiffer at 5.0 N, because the extension jumped by 4.0 cm.
options.rationale: A bigger extension per newton is read as the spring becoming stiffer.

mcqs.stem: In required practical activity 6, a spring hangs from a clamp stand and weights are added one at a time. Which method gives the most reliable value for the extension?

options.text: Take the spring off the stand after each weight and measure it flat on the bench.
options.rationale: Measuring on the bench feels easier, but the load is removed and the extension is lost.

options.text: Read the ruler from wherever you are sitting, since a scale reading cannot change.
options.rationale: The effect of the line of sight on a scale reading is not recognised.

options.text: Record the length of the loaded spring itself and use that as the extension.
options.rationale: Extension is confused with the length of the stretched spring.

options.text: Measure the loaded length at eye level and subtract the original length.
options.rationale: The extension is the loaded length minus the unloaded length, and reading a vertical ruler at eye level avoids parallax error.
